title: Can't Afford a Lawyer? Low-Cost Legal Help Options and Who Qualifies (2026)
description: Options when you can't afford a lawyer: legal aid income limits, limited-scope help, $25–$50 bar referral consults, clinics, payment plans and fee waivers.
h1: Can I afford a lawyer? Your options when money is tight
summary: If your household income is at or below 125% of the federal poverty guidelines ($19,950 for one person or $41,250 for a family of four in 2026, higher in Alaska and Hawaii), you may qualify for free civil legal aid from an LSC-funded program. Above that level, the main ways to cut the cost are limited-scope (unbundled) help, reduced-fee first consultations through state bar referral services, law school clinics, free online answers for qualifying users, payment plans, and court fee waivers. Injury and some benefits claims can often be handled on a contingency or capped fee.
body:
Start here: match your situation to the cheapest route

Where to look first
Your situationFirst place to try
Charged with a crime and cannot pay a lawyerAsk the court at your first appearance whether you qualify for a court-appointed lawyer or public defender. Civil legal aid programs funded by LSC generally cannot take criminal cases[1].
Civil problem (eviction, family, debt, benefits) and low incomeLegal aid. See the income limits below and the legal aid guide.
Income too high for legal aid, but a full retainer is out of reachLimited-scope help, a bar referral consult, or a law school clinic
Injured by someone elseA contingency-fee lawyer: no fee unless there is a recovery. See how contingency fees work.
Denied Social Security disabilityA representative under the SSA fee agreement process, where the fee is capped at the lesser of 25% of past-due benefits or $9,200[2]
Someone owes you a modest sumSmall claims court, designed for people without lawyers

1. Free legal aid, if you qualify

Programs funded by the Legal Services Corporation set their own income ceilings, which may not exceed 125% of the federal poverty guidelines unless an exception applies[3]. For 2026 in the 48 contiguous states and DC, that ceiling is $19,950 a year for one person, $27,050 for two, $34,150 for three and $41,250 for four; the figures are higher in Alaska and Hawaii[4]. Programs may accept some applicants with income up to 200% of the guidelines, for example when they seek government benefits or have high medical or dependent-care costs, and they also apply asset limits[3].

To find your local program, use LSC's address search[5] or your state's page on LawHelp.org[6]. The legal aid guide covers eligibility, what legal aid handles and a state-by-state directory.

2. Limited-scope (unbundled) help

Instead of hiring a lawyer for the whole case, you hire them for specific tasks, such as reviewing your court papers, drafting one document or coaching you before a hearing, and handle the rest yourself[7]. Rules on limited-scope work, especially court appearances, vary by state, so ask the lawyer what they can and cannot do in your court.

Example. Using Clio's 2025 national average rate of $349 an hour[8] for illustration: 3 hours of document review and hearing coaching = 3 × $349 = $1,047, compared with 30 hours of full representation = 30 × $349 = $10,470. Your actual savings depend on how much of the work you can realistically do yourself.

3. Reduced-fee consultations through a state bar

Many state bar referral services cap the first meeting with a lawyer. Examples: 30 minutes for $25 or less through the Illinois State Bar Association[9], not more than $30 through the Pennsylvania Bar Association[10], and $50 through the North Carolina Bar Association[11]. A short paid consult can tell you whether you need a lawyer at all. See the consultation fee guide for more states and what to ask.

4. Free online answers from volunteer lawyers

ABA Free Legal Answers lets qualifying users in participating states post civil legal questions, which volunteer lawyers answer at no cost and without taking on long-term representation[12]. It is useful for a specific question, such as what a notice means or whether a deadline applies, not for someone to represent you.

5. Law school clinics and pro bono programs

Many law schools run clinics in which students, supervised by licensed faculty, handle real cases at no charge, often in housing, immigration, consumer, family or small business matters. Clinics usually take a limited number of cases and follow the academic calendar, so contact them early. Local bar associations and legal aid programs also run volunteer (pro bono) lawyer programs; ask your legal aid program for a referral if it cannot take your case itself.

6. Payment plans and fee structures that fit a budget

  • Ask whether the lawyer accepts monthly payments, and get the schedule in the fee agreement.
  • Ask for a flat fee for a defined stage so the cost cannot grow without your agreement. See hourly vs. flat fee.
  • Be careful with high-interest financing: compare the annual percentage rate before you borrow to pay a retainer.
  • Government fees can sometimes be spread out too. In bankruptcy, individuals may ask the court to pay the filing fee in installments[13].

7. Court fee waivers

If the filing fee itself is the barrier, ask for a waiver:

  • Federal court: you can ask to proceed without prepaying fees by filing a sworn statement of your assets and inability to pay[14].
  • Chapter 7 bankruptcy: the fee can be waived if your income is below 150% of the poverty guidelines and you cannot pay even in installments[13].
  • State courts: every state has its own process. In California, for example, you can qualify through public benefits, household income or inability to cover basic needs, using form FW-001[15]. Your court's self-help center has the local form.

8. Cases where the other side may pay the fees

Normally each side pays its own lawyer. Some laws change that: in civil rights cases, for example, a court may award a reasonable attorney's fee to the prevailing party[16]. Lawyers sometimes take these cases at reduced or deferred cost because of that possibility. A fee award is never guaranteed, so read any agreement for what you owe if the court does not award fees.

Before you pay anyone

  • Check that the person is a licensed lawyer in your state using the state bar's online lawyer search.
  • Get the scope, the fee and any payment plan in writing before work starts.
  • Be wary of anyone who asks for cash up front, will not give you a written agreement, or promises a particular result.
  • Keep copies of everything you sign and every receipt.

faq.q: Is there free legal help for people who are not low-income?
faq.a: Full free representation is mostly limited to legal aid clients, but anyone can use court self-help centers, many law libraries and some volunteer programs. Bar referral services and limited-scope lawyers lower the cost rather than eliminate it.

faq.q: Will a court appoint a free lawyer in a civil case?
faq.a: Usually not automatically. In federal court, a judge may ask a lawyer to represent someone who cannot afford one, but that is at the court's discretion. Some states provide counsel in specific civil matters, so ask the court clerk or your legal aid program.

faq.q: Can I pay a lawyer in installments?
faq.a: Many lawyers accept payment plans if you ask before signing. Put the schedule and what happens if you miss a payment in the written fee agreement.

It is an arrangement where a lawyer handles only specific parts of your matter, such as reviewing documents or preparing you for a hearing, while you handle the rest. It costs less because you pay only for the tasks you choose.

faq.q: Can I get my court filing fee waived?
faq.a: Often, yes, if your income is low. Federal courts accept a sworn statement that you cannot pay, Chapter 7 bankruptcy fees can be waived below 150% of the poverty guidelines, and each state court has its own fee waiver form; ask the clerk or the court self-help center.
